claim: The Weber-Fechner law proposes that perceived sensory input increases with physical input on a logarithmic scale.
source: The Weber-Fechner law proposes that our perceived sensory input increases with physical input on a logarithmic scale.
evidence: This is a statement about an established scientific law, supported by citation to Fechner (1860) in the introduction.

claim: Hippocampal 'time cells' fire sequentially during a circumscribed period of time after a triggering stimulus.
source: Hippocampal 'time cells' carry a record of recent experience by firing sequentially during a circumscribed period of time after a triggering stimulus.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on time cells in the introduction and results sections.

claim: Different time cells have 'time fields' at different delays up to at least tens of seconds.
source: Different cells have 'time fields' at different delays up to at least tens of seconds.
evidence: This is supported by references to prior time cell literature and the experimental design using an 8-second delay.

claim: Past studies suggest that time cells represent a compressed timeline by demonstrating that fewer time cells fire late in the delay and their time fields are wider.
source: Past studies suggest that time cells represent a compressed timeline by demonstrating that fewer time cells fire late in the delay and their time fields are wider.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous time cell studies mentioned throughout the manuscript.

claim: After isolating across-trial variability, time field width increased linearly with delay.
source: After isolating across-trial variability, time field width increased linearly with delay.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the hierarchical Bayesian analysis and regression results presented in Figure 5b.

claim: The time cell population was distributed evenly along a logarithmic time axis.
source: Further, the time cell population was distributed evenly along a logarithmic time axis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the power-law distribution analysis with α≈1 shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The neural temporal representation in rodent hippocampus is logarithmically compressed and obeys a neural Weber-Fechner Law.
source: These findings provide strong quantitative evidence that the neural temporal representation in rodent hippocampus is logarithmically compressed and obeys a neural Weber-Fechner Law.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the data showing linear increase in time field width with delay and power-law distribution with α≈1.

claim: The Weber-Fechner law provides a good description of perceptual phenomena.
source: The Weber-Fechner law provides a good description of a wide range of phenomena in psychology including perceptual phenomena (Moore, 2012), the non-verbal numerosity system (Feigenson et al., 2004; Gallistel and Gelman, 2000), and psychological studies of time perception (Rakitin et al., 1998; Gibbon et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The representation of visual space in the retina and early visual cortical regions is logarithmically compressed as a function of distance from the fovea.
source: It has long been known that the representation of visual space in the retina and early visual cortical regions do not map visual space veridically. Rather, the representation of visual space is logarithmically compressed as a function of distance from the fovea (Schwartz, 1980; Van Essen et al., 1984; Glezer, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on visual system organization.

claim: Neurons in monkey parietal cortex recorded during numerosity judgements have receptive fields organized as a function of the logarithm of numerosity.
source: Moreover, neurons in monkey parietal cortex recorded during numerosity judgements have receptive fields organized as a function of the logarithm of numerosity (Nieder and Miller, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nieder and Miller, 2003.

claim: Unipolar brush cells in the cerebellum form a logarithmically-compressed set of temporal basis functions.
source: A recent paper from a cerebellar slice preparation argues that unipolar brush cells form a logarithmically-compressed set of temporal basis functions (Guo et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2021.

claim: Time cells in the hippocampus fire sequentially during unfilled delay intervals.
source: So-called "time cells" in the hippocampus fire sequentially during unfilled delay intervals (Pastalkova et al., 2008; MacDonald et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational time cell papers.

claim: One can reconstruct the time at which the delay began from time cell sequences.
source: Because the sequence is reliable across trials, one can reconstruct the time at which the delay began (e.g. Mau et al., 2018) and, in many cases, the identity of a stimulus that initiated the delay (Taxidis et al., 2020; Cruzado et al., 2020) such that at the population level hippocampal time cells construct a record of what happened when (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: The accuracy of the representation of time within the delay decreases with the passage of time.
source: It is well-established that time cells do not provide a veridical record of the past; rather the accuracy of the representation of time within the delay decreases with the passage of time (Kraus et al., 2013; Mau et al., 2018; Taxidis et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior time cell studies.

claim: Logarithmic compression leads to receptive field size growing linearly with distance from the fovea in the visual system.
source: First, the size of receptive fields grows linearly with distance from the fovea (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Gattass et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to visual neuroscience studies.

claim: The number of cells with receptive fields in a region of visual space goes down as the inverse of distance from the fovea.
source: Second, the number of cells with receptive fields in a region of visual space goes down as the inverse of distance from the fovea (Daniel and Whitteridge, 1961; Hubel and Wiesel, 1974; Van Essen et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classic visual neuroscience studies.

claim: It is conceivable that the increase in receptive field width is simply an averaging artifact due to variability in receptive field location across trials.
source: It is conceivable that the increase in receptive field width is simply an averaging artifact due to variability in receptive field location across trials (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a methodological concern raised by the authors, illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: Rats performed a delayed-matching task wherein each of the four study objects indicated which of the two test objects contained hidden reward.
source: Rats performed a delayed-matching task wherein each of the four study objects indicated which of the two test objects contained hidden reward.
evidence: This describes the experimental task, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Rats learned the memory task well with accuracy between 70 and 80%.
source: Rats learned the memory task well with accuracy between 70 and 80%.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: There was very little variability in positions or other measurable changes in behavior after the first two seconds of the delay.
source: There was very little variability in positions or other measurable changes in behavior after the first two seconds of the delay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, detailed analysis in Supplemental section S1).
evidence: This is a behavioral observation supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among the total of 625 pyramidal CA1 units recorded, 159 units were classified as time cells.
source: Among the total of 625 pyramidal CA1 units we recorded from the four animals, 159 units (30/87 for rat 1; 39/134 for rat 2; 32/111 for rat 3; 58/293 for rat 4) were classified as time cells using previous methods (Tiganj et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a data summary from the recordings.

claim: The proportion of time cells is similar to previous studies using similar methods.
source: The proportion of time cells is similar to previous studies using similar methods (e.g. Salz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by citation.

claim: A total of 131 robust time cells were considered for the hierarchical Bayesian analyses.
source: A total of 131 robust time cells were considered further for the hierarchical Bayesian analyses.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used for analysis.

claim: The Main Model provided the best quantitative description of the data.
source: The Main Model provided the best quantitative description of the data (see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by WAIC values in Table 1 showing the Main Model has the lowest WAIC.

claim: The Main Model revealed a high degree of variability in the estimated time field location from trial to trial.
source: The Main Model revealed a high degree of variability in the estimated time field location from trial to trial.
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical Bayesian model fitting.

claim: For some time cells, the time difference between the rat entering the treadmill and breaking the laser beam was positively correlated with the location of time field peak from trial to trial.
source: For some time cells, we found the time difference between the rat entering the treadmill and breaking the laser beam was positively correlated with the location of time field peak from trial to trial.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: About 54% of the posterior density for α is between the value of 0.9 and 1.1.
source: Furthermore, about 54% of the posterior density is between the value of 0.9 and 1.1.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the posterior distribution.

claim: The posterior distribution of α conclusively argues against uniformly distributed time cells as it excludes zero by approximately five standard deviations.
source: This posterior conclusively argues against uniformly distributed time cells as it excludes zero by approximately five standard deviations.
evidence: This is an inference from the posterior distribution data.

claim: Variability in position, running speed, and angular acceleration was much larger early in the delay and decreased dramatically after about 2 s.
source: While it is in principle difficult to assess this question as we cannot measure every possible variable that could be of interest to the animal, we can rule out confounds with observable behavior. In this experiment, animals were not perfectly still as they ran on the treadmill over the 8 s delay. However, variability in position, running speed, and angular acceleration was much larger early in the delay as the animal moved towards the edge of the treadmill. Variance in these variables decreased dramatically after about 2 s (see Supplementary section S1).
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the data.

claim: Both early (before 2s) and late (after 2s) time cell groups showed evidence of temporal compression when considered separately.
source: To assess the concern that the apparent logarithmic compression over the 8 s delay was an artifact of behavioral changes during that interval, we sorted time cells into two distinct groups with peak times before and after 2 s. Fortuitously, these groups included about the same number of time cells; the early group included 63 time cells and the late group 68. Both groups showed evidence of temporal compression when considered separately.
evidence: This is a finding from subgroup analysis.

claim: The hierarchical Bayesian model describes the firing patterns simultaneously at the individual trial level, the individual cell level, and the population level.
source: The present study analyzed a group of hippocampal CA1 time cells with a hierarchical Bayesian model that describes the firing patterns simultaneously at the individual trial level, the individual cell level, and the population level.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Within-trial time field width increased linearly with delay (Equation 3).
source: First, analysis at the individual cell level, with variability across trials removed, showed that within-trial time field width increased linearly with delay (Equation 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the hierarchical Bayesian analysis.

claim: The distribution of time field peaks followed a power-law with exponent close to one (Equation 4).
source: Second, the distribution of time field peaks followed a power-law with exponent close to one (Equation 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the hierarchical Bayesian analysis.

claim: At least some of the variability in time field location across trials was attributable to variability in the time of events at the beginning of each trial.
source: In addition to these findings at the cell and population levels, there was also substantial variability in time field location across trials. At least some of this variability was attributable to variability in the time of events at the beginning of each trial as the animal advanced onto the treadmill and began to run.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis between behavioral events and time field locations.

claim: Many previous papers have shown compression of hippocampal time cells in rodent hippocampus consistent with log compression.
source: Many previous papers have shown compression of hippocampal time cells in rodent hippocampus consistent with log compression (e.g. Kraus et al., 2013; Mau et al., 2018; Taxidis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of prior literature supported by citations.

claim: Qualitatively similar compression has been reported for sequentially activated cells in rodent striatum.
source: In addition, a qualitatively similar compression has been reported for sequentially activated cells in rodent striatum (Mello et al., 2015; Akhlaghpour et al., 2016; Parker et al., 2022), rodent MEC (Kraus et al., 2015), rodent mPFC (Tiganj et al., 2017), monkey caudate nucleus and DLPFC (Jin et al., 2009), monkey lPFC (Tiganj et al., 2018; Cruzado et al., 2020) and monkey hippocampus (Cruzado et al., 2020) during a broad variety of behavioral tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of prior literature supported by citations.

claim: Tsao et al., 2018 observed cells in rodent LEC that gradually changed their firing rate with a wide range of time constants spanning up to several minutes.
source: Recording from rodent LEC in a spatial exploration task, Tsao et al., 2018 observed cells that gradually changed their firing rate with a wide range of time constants spanning up to several minutes.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: Bright et al., 2020 observed similar results in monkey EC during a free viewing task with cells triggered by onset of an image and decaying with time constants ranging from a few hundred ms up to several s.
source: Bright et al., 2020 observed similar results in monkey EC during a free viewing task with cells triggered by onset of an image and decaying with time constants ranging from a few hundred ms up to several s.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: Dannenberg et al., 2019 found that different speed cells in rodent MEC appeared to filter the speed signal with a wide range of time constants.
source: Dannenberg et al., 2019 recorded from speed cells in rodent MEC. During exploration speed changes continuously; that study asked over what time scale filtering the speed signal provided the best account of each speed cell's time course of firing. Rather than finding a single value, different speed cells appeared to filter the speed signal with a wide range of time constants.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: Slowly-inactivating currents in EC observed in slice experiments are an attractive candidate for the graded heterogeneity of time constants in EC.
source: Although there are many possible biological mechanisms for graded heterogeneity of time constants, slowly-inactivating currents in EC observed in slice experiments (Egorov et al., 2002) are an attractive candidate for the graded heterogeneity of time constants in EC (Tiganj et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about biological mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Guo et al., 2021 reported that unipolar brush cells in the cerebellum form a logarithmically-compressed temporal basis set in a slice preparation.
source: Guo et al., 2021 reported that unipolar brush cells in the cerebellum form a logarithmically-compressed temporal basis set in a slice preparation.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: There is evidence suggesting that place fields cluster relative to landmarks in the environment.
source: There is evidence suggesting that place fields cluster relative to landmarks in the environment, such as the beginning of a path (Bjerknes et al., 2018; Sheehan et al., 2021) and edges of an open-field environment (Harland et al., 2021), a result analogous to the compression of time observed here.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work on spatial coding supported by citations.

claim: Sheehan et al., 2021 found that place fields were more numerous and more narrow closer to the landmark controlling their firing than further away from the landmark.
source: Consistent with the results from time cell experiments, place fields tiled the distance around the box smoothly. Moreover, place fields were more numerous and more narrow closer to the landmark controlling their firing than further away from the landmark (Sheehan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: The spatial frequency of grid cells falls into discrete groups that are anatomically organized.
source: It has long been appreciated that the spatial frequency of grid cells falls into discrete groups that are anatomically organized (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work on grid cells supported by citation.

claim: The relative ratio between the spatial frequency of adjacent clusters of grid cells is constant, as predicted by a normative account of spatial coding.
source: Interestingly, the relative ratio between the spatial frequency of adjacent clusters of grid cells is constant, as predicted by a normative account of spatial coding (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: Only logarithmic functions give rise to scale-covariance.
source: It can be shown that only logarithmic functions give rise to this form of scale-covariance.
evidence: This is a mathematical property stated as fact.

claim: Mello et al., 2015 observed cells in the striatum that fire sequentially in a fixed interval operant conditioning task, and when the fixed interval changed, the sequences were stretched in time.
source: For instance, Mello et al., 2015 observed cells in the striatum that fire sequentially in a fixed interval operant conditioning task. In the fixed interval procedure, the first response after a particular interval has past is reinforced. Animals learn to respond at appropriate times. Mello et al., 2015 observed that when the fixed interval changed, the sequences were stretched in time.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: Jacques et al., 2022 trained a deep network with logarithmically-compressed time cells at each layer to learn to classify auditory patterns, and after training the network recognized digits spoken much more slowly or quickly than the training examples without retraining.
source: Jacques et al., 2022 trained a deep network with logarithmically-compressed time cells at each layer to learn to classify auditory patterns (Jacques et al., 2021). After being trained to classify digits spoken at a normal rate, the network built from logarithmically-compressed time cells recognizes digits spoken much more slowly or quickly than the training examples without retraining.
evidence: This is a summary of prior computational work supported by citations.

claim: It has been argued that time constants in the early auditory system have a logarithmic distribution.
source: Notably, it has been argued that time constants in the early auditory system have a logarithmic distribution (Rahman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: Jansson and Lindeberg, 2022 used a similar idea to build networks for visual pattern classification that generalize to images that are larger or smaller than the training set.
source: Jansson and Lindeberg, 2022 used a similar idea, building on longstanding theoretical work in the context of computer vision (Lindeberg and Fagerström, 1996; Lindeberg, 2016), to build networks for visual pattern classification that generalize to images that are larger or smaller than the training set.
evidence: This is a summary of prior computational work supported by citations.

claim: In the presence of white noise, a logarithmic temporal code equalizes the mutual information between adjacent receptors.
source: For instance, in the presence of white noise, a logarithmic temporal code equalizes the mutual information between adjacent receptors (Shankar and Howard, 2013; Hsu and Marzen, 2020 see also Howard and Shankar, 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical result supported by citations.

claim: Human episodic memory has long been thought to depend on recovery of a prior state of a gradually changing state of spatiotemporal context.
source: Human episodic memory—the vivid recollection of a specific event from one's life—has long been thought to depend on recovery of a prior state of a gradually changing state of spatiotemporal context (Tulving and Madigan, 1970).
evidence: This is a summary of a theoretical framework supported by citation.

claim: The contiguity effect in episodic memory is observed across a very wide range of time scales.
source: Remarkably, the contiguity effect in episodic memory is observed across a very wide range of time scales.
evidence: This is a summary of empirical findings in human memory research, supported by subsequent citations.

claim: In a typical free recall task in which words are presented one per second, a robust contiguity effect is observed.
source: For instance, in the free recall task recall of a word from a sequentially-presented list tends to be followed by recall of a word from a nearby position within the list (Kahana, 1996). In a typical free recall task in which the words are presented one per second, a robust contiguity effect is observed (Kahana, 2008).
evidence: This is a summary of empirical findings supported by citations.

claim: If one inserts a distractor-filled delay of sixteen seconds between each word in free recall, a contiguity effect is still observed.
source: However, if one inserts a distractor-filled delay of sixteen seconds between each word, presumably clearing the contents of short-term memory between each list item, a contiguity effect is still observed (Howard and Kahana, 1999).
evidence: This is a summary of empirical findings supported by citation.

claim: There is a contiguity effect across lists when participants recall all words from all lists at the end of an experimental session.
source: If, at the end of an experimental session lasting tens of minutes, the experimenter asks the participant to recall all the words from all the lists, there is a contiguity effect across lists, despite the fact that the words from different lists are separated by hundreds of seconds (Unsworth, 2008; Howard et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a summary of empirical findings supported by citations.

claim: The contiguity effect can be observed when stimuli are presented separated by an hour.
source: At even longer scales, the contiguity effect can be observed when stimuli are presented separated by an hour (Cortis Mack et al., 2017) or when participants recall news events extended over weeks and months (Uitvlugt and Healey, 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of empirical findings supported by citations.

claim: Time cells and place cells are an appealing candidate for a neural implementation of a representation of spatiotemporal context.
source: Time cells and place cells are an appealing candidate for a neural implementation of a representation of spatiotemporal context (Howard et al., 2015; Eichenbaum, 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Logarithmic compression of time offers a solution to the theoretical problem of scale-invariant attractor dynamics.
source: Logarithmic compression of time—and the scale-covariance that follows from this property—offers a solution to this theoretical problem.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the properties of logarithmic compression.

claim: Rescaling of time translates the covariance matrix between time cells along the log time axis.
source: Rescaling of time translates the covariance matrix between time cells (up to a constant factor) along the log time axis.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of logarithmic compression.

claim: If the covariance matrix can be shaped to form a line attractor, this would enable retrieval of logarithmically-compressed states of spatiotemporal context.
source: If the covariance matrix can be shaped to form a line attractor (Spalla et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2020; Chaudhuri et al., 2019) this would enable retrieval of logarithmically-compressed states of spatiotemporal context.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Time cell sequences may continue much longer than the eight second delay used in this experiment.
source: Although time cell sequences may continue much longer than the eight second delay used in this experiments (Shikano et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022), it is difficult to imagine that time cell sequences persist for hours and days.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limits of time cell sequences, with citations to prior work.

claim: Nielson et al., 2015 found that pattern similarity in the hippocampus fell off as a function of log time extending up to weeks.
source: For instance, Nielson et al., 2015 studied the pattern similarity across voxels in the hippocampus evoked by different real world memories. Pairs of memories were separated by objective distances in time and space. Nielson et al., 2015 found that pattern similarity fell off as a function of log time extending up to weeks.
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citation.

claim: Arzy et al., 2009 found the accuracy for the time of past events decreased linearly with log-scaled time, suggesting a logarithmically-compressed temporal representation over time scales up to decades.
source: Behaviorally, Arzy et al., 2009 asked human participants to place real world autobiographical events on a timeline centered at the present. They found the accuracy for the time of past events decreased linearly with log-scaled time, suggesting a logarithmically-compressed temporal representation over time scales up to decades (see also Peer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work supported by citations.

claim: Representational drift is a possible candidate to play the role of spatiotemporal context over autobiographical time scales.
source: Representational drift—slow changes in the pattern of active neurons when a particular stimulus or experimental setting is repeated—is a possible candidate to play the role of spatiotemporal context over autobiographical time scales (Ziv et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2016; Mau et al., 2018; Mau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Four male Long-Evans rats were used as subjects in the experiment.
source: Subjects were four male Long-Evans rats (Charles River) weighing between 350 and 450 g and between the ages of 6 months to 1.5 years for the duration of the experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: All procedures were conducted in accordance with the requirements set by the National Institutes of Health, and were approved by the Boston University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were conducted in accordance with the requirements set by the National Institutes of Health, and were approved by the Boston University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (BU IACUC).
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: The behavioral apparatus consisted of a custom-built 355 cm long by 7.5 cm wide circular track with an integrated treadmill.
source: The behavioral apparatus consisted of a custom-built 355 cm long by 7.5 cm wide circular track with an integrated treadmill using commercially available parts (Columbus Instruments).
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus.

claim: Rats were trained to sample one of two test objects before running through the treadmill platform and then choosing the matching one of two terra cotta pots discriminable by scent and digging media.
source: Then, rats were trained to sample one of two test objects before running through the treadmill platform and then choosing the matching one of two terra cotta pots discriminable by scent and digging media (Keene et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claim: Tetrodes were plated with non-cyanide gold solution via electrolysis to reduce impedance to between 180 and 220 kOhms.
source: Tetrodes were plated with non-cyanide gold solution (Neuralynx) via electrolysis using a Nano-Z (White Matter LLC) in order to reduce impedance to between 180 and 220 kOhms.
evidence: This describes the electrode preparation procedure.

claim: All electrophysiological recordings were performed using a 96 channel multichannel Acquisition Processor (MAP) recording system.
source: All electrophysiological recordings were performed using a 96 channel multichannel Acquisition Processor (MAP) recording system (Plexon).
evidence: This describes the recording equipment.

claim: Only well-isolated units (Isolation Rating > 40 L-Ratio <0.001) were kept for further analysis.
source: Only well-isolated units (Isolation Rating > 40 L-Ratio <0.001) were kept for further analysis.
evidence: This describes the spike sorting quality criteria.

claim: The posterior distributions of estimated parameters were generated through the rStan package with 8 independent Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo (MCMC) chains.
source: The posterior distributions of estimated parameters were generated through the rStan package (Stan development team, 2021) with 8 independent Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo (MCMC) chains (4800 warm-up iterations and 200 post warm-up samples in each of the MCMC chains).
evidence: This describes the Bayesian model fitting procedure.
